subject: Accounting
title: The Birth of GAAP
description: A quick win: understand The Birth of GAAP.

hook.text: GAAP sounds boring. But without it, every company's financials would be a guessing game.

buildup.text: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles emerged after the Depression to standardize reporting.

discovery.text: GAAP defines how revenue, expenses, assets, and liabilities must be measured and disclosed.

twist.text: GAAP isn't one document—it's thousands of rules built up over nearly a century.

climax.text: Every public company in the U.S. must follow GAAP. Violating it triggers SEC enforcement.

punchline.text: GAAP is the rulebook that makes comparisons possible.

details.summary: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles were born in the aftermath of the 1929 stock market crash, when the U.S. government demanded standardized financial reporting rules to prevent the misleading and inconsistent accounting that had contributed to the disaster.
details.whyItMatters: GAAP created a common language for financial reporting that allows investors to compare companies on equal terms, forming the foundation of transparent capital markets.
takeaways: GAAP was created after the 1929 crash to standardize previously inconsistent financial reporting
The SEC delegated accounting standard-setting to the private sector, eventually creating FASB
GAAP ensures companies follow the same rules so financial statements are comparable

faq.question: What event led to the creation of GAAP?
faq.answer: The 1929 stock market crash and subsequent Great Depression revealed that companies used wildly inconsistent accounting methods, making it impossible for investors to compare them. Congress created the SEC, which then established standardized reporting rules that became GAAP.

faq.question: Who creates and maintains GAAP?
faq.answer: The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) is the private-sector body that creates and updates GAAP in the United States. The SEC has ultimate authority but delegates standard-setting to FASB, which issues detailed rules that all public companies must follow.
